title: Course Schedule II
description: Brute force to optimized: DFS-based topological sort with reversal versus Kahn's algorithm recording the processing order directly.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given numCourses and prerequisite pairs [a, b] (b before a), return ONE valid ordering of courses that satisfies all prerequisites, or an empty array if no valid ordering exists (a cycle).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","numCourses, prerequisites"],["Output","A valid course order, or an empty array if impossible"],["Key Insight","Kahn's algorithm (BFS via in-degrees) naturally produces a valid topological order as its PROCESSING order, directly"],["Constraints","Up to 2000 courses"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Return ONE valid ordering respecting prerequisite constraints\"","Topological sort: Kahn's algorithm (BFS via in-degrees) directly produces such an ordering, or DFS with post-order reversal"]]}

blocks.text: This directly extends Course Schedule I: instead of just checking WHETHER all courses can be finished, record the ACTUAL order courses get processed in during Kahn's algorithm. Since a course only becomes eligible for processing (reaches in-degree 0) once all its prerequisites have already been processed, the resulting processing order automatically respects every prerequisite constraint.

blocks.title: Analogy: Producing an Actual Valid Task Schedule Respecting Prerequisites
blocks.text: Picture not just checking whether a set of tasks with prerequisites CAN all be completed, but producing one concrete, valid SCHEDULE listing tasks in an order that never asks for a task before its prerequisites are done. Recording tasks in the exact order they become eligible naturally produces such a schedule.

blocks.caption: The processing order in Kahn's algorithm IS a valid topological (course) order

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Building the adjacency list and in-degree array works EXACTLY as in Course Schedule I.

Observation 2: Seeding the BFS queue with every zero-in-degree course and processing it works identically as well.

Observation 3: The ONLY addition needed is to APPEND each processed course to a result list, in the exact order it gets dequeued and processed.

Observation 4: If the final result list's length equals numCourses, it is a complete, valid ordering; otherwise (some courses never got processed due to a cycle), return an empty array instead.
This leads to reusing Kahn's algorithm exactly as before, simply recording the processing order as the answer.
Use a DFS-based topological sort instead: after fully exploring a node's descendants (post-order), prepend it to the front of the result list.
Why the code is written this way

items: DFS-based topological sort correctly produces a valid order via post-order traversal and reversal.
This requires careful three-state cycle tracking AND a final reversal step; Kahn's algorithm (BFS via in-degrees) produces the order directly, in the correct direction, without needing reversal.

blocks.text: Limitation: Kahn's algorithm achieves the same complexity with simpler, more direct bookkeeping (no reversal needed, and cycle detection is a simple final count check).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build the adjacency list and in-degree array exactly as in Course Schedule I. Seed a queue with every zero-in-degree course. Process the queue: dequeue a course, APPEND it to the result list, and for each course it points to, decrement its in-degree, enqueueing it if it reaches 0. After the queue empties, if the result list's length equals numCourses, return it; otherwise, return an empty array (a cycle prevented some courses from ever being processed).
Reuse Kahn's algorithm, appending each processed course directly to the result list.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Action"],"rows":[["Initial zero in-degree","course 0"],["Process 0","result=[0], decrement 1 and 2, both reach 0, enqueue both"],["Process 1, then 2","result=[0,1,2], decrement 3 twice, reaches 0, enqueue"],["Process 3","result=[0,1,2,3], complete"]]}

blocks.text: A course only ever gets dequeued and appended to the result AFTER every one of its prerequisites has already been dequeued (its in-degree only reaches 0 once all incoming edges from prerequisites have been "consumed" by their own processing), so the resulting order automatically and correctly respects every prerequisite constraint; if a cycle exists, some courses never reach in-degree 0 at all, and the final result length falls short of numCourses, correctly signaled by returning an empty array.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(courses plus prerequisites).
Space: O(courses plus prerequisites) for the adjacency list and in-degree array.

blocks.text: Course Schedule II directly extends Course Schedule I: the processing order of Kahn's algorithm is itself a valid topological order, requiring no extra work beyond recording it.

items: Forgetting to check the final result length against numCourses, incorrectly returning a partial (invalid) order when a cycle exists.
Using the DFS-based approach without remembering to REVERSE the post-order result at the end.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "return an actual valid ordering respecting prerequisites", think: Kahn's algorithm, recording the processing order directly.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both the DFS-based and Kahn's algorithm approaches cost O(courses plus prerequisites); Kahn's algorithm is generally the more direct implementation here.

items: Pattern: topological sort via Kahn's algorithm (BFS using in-degrees).
Core Idea: the order courses get processed in during Kahn's algorithm IS a valid topological order, recorded directly.
Time: O(courses plus prerequisites) for both approaches.
Space: O(courses) recursion depth for DFS, O(courses plus prerequisites) for Kahn's algorithm.
Most Important Observation: no extra work is needed beyond recording Kahn's algorithm's processing order.
Interview Difficulty: a very frequently asked, direct extension of a foundational medium-level graph problem.
One line memory trick: record the order you process courses in.
